newsitem.title: USA: Even in death, Spiro Agnew confounds the "nabobs".
newsitem.headline: Even in death, Spiro Agnew confounds the "nabobs".

text.p: In death as in life, former U.S. vice-president Spiro Agnew managed to confound what he once called "nattering nabobs of negativism" in the media as his family balked at saying how he died.
On Wednesday, one day after Agnew died at Atlantic General Hospital in Berlin, Maryland, hospital officials said they were not authorised to release Agnew's cause of death.

It all seemed part of the Agnew legacy of defiance of the Washington establishment, especially the U.S. press, during the troubled White House tenure of Richard Nixon. At least one insider recalled that characteristic with affection.
"Spiro Agnew had something few people in this city ever show -- raw political courage," former presidential candidate and political speechwriter Pat Buchanan said in a statement.

"At a time when the establishment was craven in its pandering to rioters and demonstrators, Vice President Agnew told the truth about both of them ... He would never be forgiven for that," Buchanan said.
Some of Agnew's choicest denunciations were of those demonstrating against the Vietnam War.

Agnew's abilities as the orator of the American middle class -- he called it the "silent majority" -- left a permanent mark on the political landscape during the Nixon administration, though observers from both ends of the political spectrum were sceptical about how deep his convictions went.

"He was elected as governor (of Maryland) as a symbol of clean government," said George Callcott, history professor emeritus at the University of Maryland. "... Unfortunately, he was on the take in Baltimore County, in Maryland and probably as vice president.
"When a person calls for clean government and is asking contractors for bribes (as Agnew pleaded no contest to doing) one can't escape the note of hypocrisy," Callcott said in a telephone interview.

"He was a great actor," Washington Post columnist David Broder said on CNN. Referring to Agnew's attacks on the media as, among other things, "an effete corps of impudent snobs," Broder said, "It was just a piece of rhetoric, along with a lot of other things that ... he learned to pretend to espouse."

Columnist Robert Novak called Agnew "an incredibly corrupt figure," adding in a CNN interview: "It's sad that he for a time was the hero of the conservative movement ... He was essentially an artificial figure and I think he really had very little ideological framework."

Activist lawyer John Banzhaf of George Washington University saw another legacy: the principle that ordinary citizens may sue political figures who take bribes, payoffs and kickbacks and force them to pay back money they received illegally.

That principle was brought into play after Agnew resigned the vice presidency -- only the second person in U.S. history to do so -- in 1973 rather than stand trial on charges he extorted money while serving as governor of Maryland in 1967 and 1968. He pleaded "no contest" and was sentenced to three years probation and fined $10,000.

Ten years after he left office, a state court ordered Agnew to repay $268,482 to cover the kickbacks. The court determined, in a civil suit brought by law students at George Washington University, that Agnew had accepted $147,500 in illegal payments and ordered him to repay that plus more than $120,000 in interest.
